hook.line: The year supercomputer analysis showed that perfect play by both sides ends in a draw — an answer no one knew for over a century.
hook.say: Let me show you the story of reversi!

ch.t: Born in London, raised in Japan
ch.say: It has two homelands: Britain and Japan.
p: Reversi was a hit in 1880s Britain, and two Englishmen are said to have disputed who invented it.
In 1973, Othello, devised by Hasegawa Gorō, went on sale in Japan and spread around the world.

ch.say: Japan turned it into a world game.
tl: Sold in London as “Reversi” and becomes popular
Othello goes on sale in Japan
First world championship held in Tokyo
The program Logistello beats the world champion 6–0
Shown to be a draw with perfect play

ch.say: Everything starts from the middle four.
ch.cap: The opening position and a first move: the flanked disc flips
p: In early British reversi, players are said to have placed the first four discs wherever they liked.
Fixing them as a diagonal cross in the centre let opening theory grow rapidly.

ch.say: Change the board, change the answer!
cards: A 19th-century ancestor said to be played on a cross-shaped board
Proven by computer to be a win for the second player
The crossed centre start used at world championships

ch.say: Humans and AI had some great battles.
stats: Squares — and discs — on the board
cards: Creator of Othello, who also led the Japan Othello Association
In 1997 Logistello swept world champion Murakami Takeshi — the computer era had arrived

ch.say: Tap a card to flip it!
cards: Shakespeare’s play Othello, a story of black and white
The second player — proven by computer in the 1990s
A disc on a corner can never be flipped

ch.say: One move can turn the whole game!
p: Simple rules, gripping to the very last disc. Start from the middle four.
